reference.source: Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology / Cornea by Krachmer
clinicalPearls: A slowly progressive, non-inflammatory degeneration producing elevated bluish-white or grey subepithelial nodules, often in a ring around the mid-periphery
Frequently follows chronic ocular surface irritation or inflammation, including trachoma, chronic blepharitis, phlyctenulosis, dry eye, and contact lens wear
More common in middle-aged women and often bilateral, though asymmetric
Symptoms range from asymptomatic to foreign body sensation, irritation, and reduced vision when nodules encroach centrally or induce irregular astigmatism
Recurrent erosions can occur where nodules disturb epithelial adhesion
Histology shows subepithelial hyaline deposits with a disrupted or absent Bowman layer beneath the nodules
Management ranges from lubrication and treating the underlying surface disease to superficial keratectomy or phototherapeutic keratectomy for visually significant nodules
Nodules may recur after removal, particularly if the underlying surface disorder is not controlled
reference.pathophysiology: Salzmann nodular degeneration is a non-inflammatory degeneration in which elevated hyaline nodules form in the subepithelial space, typically as a reaction to long-standing ocular surface disease or chronic irritation. Fibrous and hyaline material accumulates between the epithelium and a disrupted Bowman layer, elevating the surface into discrete nodules. These raised lesions distort the overlying epithelium and tear film, causing foreign body sensation and inducing irregular astigmatism when they lie near the visual axis. Because the degeneration is often driven by an underlying surface disorder, control of that condition is important to limit progression and recurrence.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral corneal pannus and scarring from chronic surface disease
Pterygium or pinguecula encroaching on the cornea
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination documenting elevated subepithelial nodules and their location
Corneal topography to assess irregular astigmatism from the nodules
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography to measure nodule thickness and plane
Evaluation for underlying ocular surface disease (blepharitis, dry eye, prior inflammation)
Fluorescein staining to assess epithelial integrity and erosions
Histology of excised nodules showing subepithelial hyaline material when tissue is available
redFlags: Central nodules causing significant visual loss
Recurrent painful erosions from disrupted epithelial adhesion
Rapid enlargement or atypical appearance suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Recurrence after surgical removal indicating uncontrolled underlying surface disease
reference.prognosis: Progression is usually slow, and vision is often preserved unless nodules involve the visual axis or induce irregular astigmatism. Superficial removal generally improves symptoms, but nodules can recur if the underlying ocular surface disease is not addressed.
pitfalls: Removing nodules without treating the underlying surface disease, leading to recurrence
Mistaking nodules for a corneal dystrophy without considering the acquired degeneration
Overlooking induced irregular astigmatism as the cause of reduced vision
Aggressive keratectomy risking scarring when observation would suffice
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
management: Treatment of the underlying ocular surface disease driving the degeneration, including lid hygiene for blepharitis and control of dry eye
Ocular surface lubrication with tear substitutes to relieve foreign body sensation and irritation
Superficial keratectomy or manual nodule removal when nodules encroach on the visual axis or induce irregular astigmatism
Management of recurrent corneal erosions with lubricants, bandage contact lenses or epithelial debridement
Review and modification of contact lens wear as a contributing irritant
Corneal topography surveillance to monitor astigmatism and detect progression or recurrence
Referral to a corneal specialist for surgical removal and ongoing management where vision is threatened
